blocks.text: It was now late in the afternoon, and sunset was not far off. We had to accept that we could do no more. With heavy hearts, we agreed with the Professor when he said:—

“Let us go back to Madam Mina—poor, poor dear Madam Mina. We have done everything we can for now. At least we can protect her there. But we need not lose hope. Only one more box of earth remains, and we must try to find it. Once we have done that, everything may still turn out well.” I could see that he spoke as bravely as he could to comfort Harker. The poor man was completely overcome by sadness. From time to time, he gave a low groan that he could not hold back. He was thinking of his wife.

We returned to my house with sad hearts. There we found Mrs. Harker waiting for us. She seemed cheerful, showing how brave she was and how much she cared for others. When she saw our faces, her own face became as pale as death. For a second or two, she closed her eyes, as if praying silently. Then she said cheerfully:—

“I can never thank you all enough. Oh, my poor darling!” As she spoke, she took her husband’s grey head in her hands and kissed it. “Lay your poor head here and rest it. All will yet be well, dear! God will protect us if that is His good purpose.” The poor man groaned. His misery was so great that there was no room for words.

We ate supper together, though we took little interest in the meal. I think it cheered us all up a little. Perhaps it was simply the warmth that food brought to our hungry bodies. None of us had eaten anything since breakfast. Or perhaps being together helped us. Whatever the reason, we all felt less miserable. Tomorrow now seemed to offer at least some hope. As we had promised, we told Mrs. Harker everything that had happened. At times, she became as white as snow. This happened when we described moments when her husband had seemed to be in danger. At other times, she turned red as she heard how deeply he loved her. But she listened bravely and calmly. We reached the part where Harker had rushed at the Count without thinking of the danger. She clung to her husband’s arm and held it tight. It was as if holding him could protect him from any harm that might come. However, she said nothing until we had finished telling her everything, right up to that moment. Then she stood up among us and spoke, still holding her husband’s hand. Oh, I wish I could give some idea of that scene! There stood that sweet, sweet, good, good woman. She was young and full of life, and her beauty shone brightly. Yet there was the red scar on her forehead, which she knew was there. We ground our teeth when we saw it, remembering where it came from and how she got it. Her loving kindness stood against our fierce hatred. Her gentle faith stood against all our fears and doubts. And we knew what the mark stood for. It showed that she was shut out from God, despite all her goodness, her pure heart, and her faith.

“Jonathan,” she said. The word sounded like music on her lips, so full of love and tenderness. “Jonathan dear, and all of you, my true, true friends. I want you to remember something throughout this dreadful time. I know that you must fight. You must destroy, just as you destroyed the false Lucy so that the true Lucy could live after death. But you must not do this out of hate. That poor soul who has caused all this misery is the most unhappy of all. Just think how joyful he will be when his worse part is destroyed too. Then his better part may live for ever as a spirit. You must feel pity for him too, although that pity must not stop you from destroying him.”

As she spoke, I could see her husband’s face grow dark and tight. It was as if his strong feelings were drying and shrinking him deep inside. Without thinking, he held his wife’s hand more tightly, until his knuckles looked white. I knew this must have hurt her, but she did not pull away or show pain. Instead, her eyes seemed to beg him more strongly than ever. When she stopped speaking, he jumped to his feet. He almost tore his hand from hers as he spoke:—
